title: Vendor Risk Assessment: A Practical Review Before You Buy SaaS
description: A vendor risk assessment guide for reviewing data access, security evidence, continuity, subprocessors, contract terms, and exit plans before adopting SaaS.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Classify the Service and Its Impact
sections.body: Begin by identifying what the vendor will do and what happens if the service fails or exposes data. A public note-taking tool and a system that stores customer records or controls production access do not require identical review. Document the data categories involved, user groups, integrations, business processes supported, and the maximum tolerable outage. Classify the vendor's criticality before requesting evidence so the depth of review matches the potential impact. Record the business owner who accepts residual risk.

sections.title: Review Security Evidence Carefully
sections.body: Ask for evidence relevant to the service and contract, such as security documentation, audit reports, penetration-test summaries, vulnerability handling, incident communication, authentication controls, and access review practices. Check scope and dates: a certification or report may cover only selected services or locations. Distinguish independently assessed evidence from a vendor's self-description. Record unanswered questions and decide whether they are blockers, mitigations, or accepted limitations. Do not claim a vendor is secure merely because a logo appears on a trust page.

sections.title: Map Data, Subprocessors, and Access
sections.body: List the information the vendor receives, where it is processed, how long it is retained, and which subprocessors can access it. Review how data is encrypted in transit and at rest, how administrative access is controlled, and whether your organization can configure retention and deletion. Understand support access and emergency access procedures. If the vendor uses customer data to improve models or services, determine the available controls and whether they meet your organization's rules. Seek qualified privacy review for personal or regulated data.

sections.title: Check Identity and Operational Controls
sections.body: Verify the controls that will matter in your actual deployment.
items: Single sign-on and multi-factor authentication fit your identity requirements.
Roles can limit access by team, project, environment, or data class.
Audit logs record relevant administrative and data-access events.
Provisioning and offboarding can remove access promptly.
Secrets and integration tokens can be scoped, rotated, and revoked.
Security notifications have a named recipient and response process.
The vendor documents backup, recovery, and incident escalation responsibilities.

sections.title: Assess Continuity and Support
sections.body: Review service commitments, maintenance windows, support response definitions, backup practices, recovery objectives, and status communication. Ask how the service behaves during a regional outage or a failure in a critical dependency. Confirm whether support is available at the times your team needs it and whether escalation routes are included in the selected plan. Treat a stated service-level target as a contractual commitment only when the contract says so. For critical services, identify a workable manual process or alternate path for essential operations.

sections.title: Review Contract, Renewal, and Exit
sections.body: Check data processing terms, confidentiality, breach notification, liability, renewal notice periods, price changes, ownership of customer data, and restrictions on export. Understand whether you can retrieve records, attachments, configurations, logs, and relationships in a usable format. Estimate the time and cost of migration and deletion verification. Avoid leaving exit planning until a dispute or renewal deadline. Keep a record of the contract version, approved exceptions, and the person authorized to accept them.

sections.title: Score and Reassess the Risk
sections.body: Use a consistent risk register with likelihood, impact, existing controls, evidence, owner, mitigation, and a due date. Do not let a numeric score conceal a critical unresolved issue; define hard blockers separately. Review the vendor again when data sensitivity increases, a new integration is added, the contract changes, or a significant incident occurs. Keep evidence current and make the decision traceable: approve, approve with conditions, request more evidence, or reject. The goal is a proportionate decision, not a paperwork exercise.
